q: the daughter of Alcinous stood firm, for Minerva put courage into her heart and took away all fear from her.

s: Nausicaa travels with Nausicaa's maids (to wash clothes)
q: They pulled without flagging, and carried not only Nausicaa and her wash of clothes, but the maids also who were with her.

s: Nausicaa's maids are servants (of Nausicaa’s household)
q: Two maid servants were sleeping near her, both very pretty, one on either side of the doorway, which was closed with well made folding doors.

s: Nausicaa's maids accompany Nausicaa (on the washing excursion)
q: They pulled without flagging, and carried not only Nausicaa and her wash of clothes, but the maids also who were with her.

s: Minerva assists Ulysses (in returning home)
q: To his house, then, did Minerva hie in furtherance of the return of Ulysses.

s: Phaeacians are seafaring folk (proud of their masts, oars, and ships)
q: for the Phaeacians are not a nation of archers; they know nothing about bows and arrows, but are a sea-faring folk, and pride themselves on their masts, oars, and ships, with which they travel far over the sea.

s: Phaeacians live apart from other people (on a land’s end jutting into the sea)
q: we are dear to the gods, and live apart on a land’s end that juts into the sounding sea, and have nothing to do with any other people.

s: Alcinous is a king (of the Phaeacians)
q: and King Alcinous, whose counsels were inspired of heaven, was now reigning.

s: Alcinous rules Phaeacians (the whole power of the state is vested in him)
q: we are called Phaeacians, and I am daughter to Alcinous, in whom the whole power of the state is vested.

s: Alcinous is father of Nausicaa
q: Nausicaa, daughter to King Alcinous.

s: Scheria is a land (settled by the Phaeacians far from other people)
q: so their king Nausithous moved them thence and settled them in Scheria, far from all other people.

s: Scheria contains Phaeacian city (surrounded by a wall)
q: He surrounded the city with a wall, built houses and temples, and divided the lands among his people;

s: Phaeacian city has harbours (one on either side with narrow entrances)
q: you will find a high wall running all round it, and a good harbour on either side with a narrow entrance into the city,

s: Phaeacian city contains Phaeacian ships (drawn up by the roadside)
q: and the ships will be drawn up by the road side, for every one has a place where his own ship can lie.

s: Minerva takes the form of Dymas (Dymas’s daughter and Nausicaa’s bosom friend)
q: Minerva took the form of the famous sea captain Dymas’s daughter, who was a bosom friend of Nausicaa and just her own age;

s: waggon carries clothes (to the washing cisterns)
q: the girl brought the clothes down from the linen room and placed them on the waggon.

s: mules feed on herbage (by the water side)
q: Here they unharnessed the mules and turned them out to feed on the sweet juicy herbage that grew by the water side.

s: clothes are washed at the pits
q: Here they unharnessed the mules and turned them out to feed on the sweet juicy herbage that grew by the water side. They took the clothes out of the waggon, put them in the water, and vied with one another in treading them in the pits to get the dirt out.

s: washing cisterns contain pure water (available at all times)
q: through which there ran at all times enough pure water to wash any quantity of linen, no matter how dirty.

s: sea takes me (all the way from the Ogygian island)
q: yesterday made the twentieth day that I had been tossing about upon the sea. The winds and waves have taken me all the way from the Ogygian island,

s: Ulysses's shipwreck and wanderings begins at the Ogygian island (from which the winds and waves carried Ulysses)
q: The winds and waves have taken me all the way from the Ogygian island,

s: Ulysses is tossed about upon the sea
q: yesterday made the twentieth day that I had been tossing about upon the sea.

s: Minerva dwells on Olympus (as the everlasting home of the gods)
q: When she had said this Minerva went away to Olympus, which they say is the everlasting home of the gods.

s: Phaeacian hospitality provides clothes (to a foreigner in distress)
q: Now, however, that you have come to this our country, you shall not want for clothes nor for anything else that a foreigner in distress may reasonably look for.

s: Phaeacian hospitality protects foreigners in distress (under Jove’s protection)
q: strangers and foreigners in distress are under Jove’s protection, and will take what they can get and be thankful;

s: marriage is a desired future state (for Nausicaa and her suitor)
q: for all the best young men among your own people are courting you, and you are not going to remain a maid much longer.

s: marriage provides peaceful home (when husband and wife are of one mind)
q: for there is nothing better in this world than that man and wife should be of one mind in a house.

s: Minerva protects Nausicaa (by giving her courage)
q: On seeing one so unkempt and so begrimed with salt water, the others scampered off along the spits that jutted out into the sea, but the daughter of Alcinous stood firm, for Minerva put courage into her heart and took away all fear from her.

s: Minerva makes Ulysses (appear taller, stronger, younger, and handsome)
q: Minerva then made him look taller and stronger than before, she also made the hair grow thick on the top of his head, and flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms;

s: Minerva's sacred grove is a sacred grove (dedicated to Minerva)
q: you will see a beautiful grove of poplars by the road side dedicated to Minerva; it has a well in it and a meadow all round it.

s: Nausicaa is daughter of King Alcinous
q: Nausicaa, daughter to King Alcinous.

s: Nausicaa is lovely (as a goddess)
q: slept a girl who was as lovely as a goddess, Nausicaa, daughter to King Alcinous

s: Ulysses is a suppliant (at Alcinous's hearth)
q: “Queen Arete,” he exclaimed, “daughter of great Rhexenor, in my distress I humbly pray you, as also your husband and these your guests (whom may heaven prosper with long life and happiness, and may they leave their possessions to their children, and all the honours conferred upon them by the state) to help me home to my own country as soon as possible; for I have been long in trouble and away from my friends.”

s: Nausicaa is a daughter of Alcinous
q: Stranger,” replied Alcinous, “I am not the kind of man to get angry about nothing; it is always better to be reasonable; but by Father Jove, Minerva, and Apollo, now that I see what kind of person you are, and how much you think as I do, I wish you would stay here, marry my daughter, and become my son-in-law.

s: Nausicaa gives Ulysses's clothes (after his washing)
q: She gave me plenty of bread and wine, and when she had had me washed in the river she also gave me the clothes in which you see me.

s: Alcinous is a king of the Phaeacians
q: This old woman had been brought by sea from Apeira, and had been chosen as a prize for Alcinous because he was king over the Phaeacians, and the people obeyed him as though he were a god

s: Alcinous descends from Neptune
q: They both descend originally from Neptune, who was father to Nausithous by Periboea, a woman of great beauty.

s: Alcinous offers Odyssey homeward voyage (to his home or chosen destination)
q: during the whole voyage if you like, and the men shall sail you over smooth waters either to your own home, or wherever you please

s: Arete is respected by Phaeacians (beyond measure)
q: Thus she both was, and still is, respected beyond measure by her children, by Alcinous himself, and by the whole people

s: Arete is a good woman (in head and heart)
q: for she is a thoroughly good woman both in head and heart, and when any women are friends of hers, she will help their husbands also to settle their disputes.

s: Arete recognizes Ulysses's clothes (as made by herself and her maids)
q: Arete was the first to speak, for she recognised the shirt, cloak, and good clothes that Ulysses was wearing, as the work of herself and of her maids

s: Ulysses is a foreign stranger (in distress)
q: “My dear, will you be so kind as to show me the house of king Alcinous? I am an unfortunate foreigner in distress, and do not know one in your town and country.”

s: Phaeacians are sea-faring folk (skilled sailors)
q: They are a sea-faring folk, and sail the seas by the grace of Neptune in ships that glide along like thought, or as a bird in the air.

s: Phaeacians excel at seafaring (best sailors in the world)
q: As the Phaeacians are the best sailors in the world, so their women excel all others in weaving

s: Phaeacian seafaring excel all others
q: You will thus see how much my ships excel all others, and what magnificent oarsmen my sailors are.

s: palace of King Alcinous contains golden and silver mastiffs (guarding the palace)
q: On either side there stood gold and silver mastiffs which Vulcan, with his consummate skill, had fashioned expressly to keep watch over the palace of king Alcinous

s: Ulysses seeks Ulysses's return (from the Phaeacians)
q: As for yourselves, do as you propose, and at break of day set about helping me to get home.

s: Neptune is father of Nausithous (by Periboea)
q: Neptune, however, lay with his daughter, and she had a son by him, the great Nausithous, who reigned over the Phaeacians.

s: Nausithous is father of Alcinous (king of the Phaeacians)
q: Nausithous had two sons Rhexenor and Alcinous

s: Calypso is a goddess (daughter of Atlas)
q: Here dwells the cunning and powerful goddess Calypso, daughter of Atlas.

s: Calypso keeps Ulysses (on Ogygian island for seven years)
q: I stayed with Calypso seven years straight on end, and watered the good clothes she gave me with my tears during the whole time

s: Ulysses's raft is sent by Calypso (provisioned for departure)
q: She sent me from her island on a raft, which she provisioned with abundance of bread and wine.

s: Ulysses survives Ulysses's shipwreck and wanderings (after losing his comrades)
q: My brave comrades were drowned every man of them, but I stuck to the keel and was carried hither and thither for the space of nine days

s: sacrificial banquet is planned by Alcinous (in honour of Ulysses)
q: To-morrow morning I shall invite a still larger number of aldermen, and will give a sacrificial banquet in honour of our guest

s: hospitality to suppliants protects suppliants (under Jove's protection)
q: make a drink offering to Jove the lord of thunder, who takes all well disposed suppliants under his protection

s: Ulysses is sent from her island (on a raft)
q: She sent me from her island on a raft, which she provisioned with abundance of bread and wine. Moreover she gave me good stout clothing, and sent me a wind that blew both warm and fair.

s: Minerva is a goddess (protective of Ulysses)
q: Then Minerva said, “Yes, father stranger, I will show you the house you want, for Alcinous lives quite close to my own father.

s: Minerva disguises as a little girl (carrying a pitcher)
q: Then, as he was just entering the town, she came towards him in the likeness of a little girl carrying a pitcher.

s: Minerva teaches Phaeacian women (useful arts)
q: As the Phaeacians are the best sailors in the world, so their women excel all others in weaving, for Minerva has taught them all manner of useful arts, and they are very intelligent.

s: Ulysses excels at disc (throwing farther than the Phaeacians)
q: Then, swinging it back, he threw it from his brawny hand, and it made a humming sound in the air as he did so. The Phaeacians quailed beneath the rushing of its flight as it sped gracefully from his hand, and flew beyond any mark that had been made yet.

s: Ulysses is skilled at archery (among living men)
q: I am an excellent archer. In battle I am always the first to bring a man down with my arrow, no matter how many more are taking aim at him alongside of me.

s: Ulysses is compared with Philoctetes (Philoctetes shoots better than Ulysses)
q: Philoctetes was the only man who could shoot better than I could when we Achaeans were before Troy and in practice.

s: Ulysses is compared with Hercules (Ulysses does not claim superiority over the mighty dead)
q: I should not like to shoot against the mighty dead, such as Hercules, or Eurytus the Oechalian—men who could shoot against the gods themselves.

s: Ulysses seeks Ulysses's return (with Phaeacian assistance)
q: I have been through infinite trouble, and am come among you now as a suppliant, praying your king and people to further me on my return home.

s: Minerva assists Ulysses (by helping him obtain passage home)
q: while Minerva took the form of one of Alcinous’ servants, and went round the town in order to help Ulysses to get home.

s: Minerva (in disguise) is a servant (of Alcinous)
q: while Minerva took the form of one of Alcinous’ servants

s: Minerva (in disguise) marks disc (where Ulysses's throw landed)
q: Minerva, in the form of a man, came and marked the place where it had fallen.

s: Phaeacians are fond of good dinners, music, and dancing (also like frequent changes of linen, warm baths, and good beds)
q: We are extremely fond of good dinners, music, and dancing; we also like frequent changes of linen, warm baths, and good beds

s: Phaeacians are excellent sailors
q: We are not particularly remarkable for our boxing, nor yet as wrestlers, but we are singularly fleet of foot and are excellent sailors.

s: Phaeacian aldermen and town councillors participate in sacrificial banquet (with Alcinous and Ulysses)
q: you aldermen and town councillors, you will join me in entertaining our guest in the cloisters.

s: Phaeacian ship is a ship (new and not previously voyaged)
q: Let us draw a ship into the sea—one that has never yet made a voyage

s: Phaeacian ship is manned by Phaeacian sailors (fifty-two oarsmen)
q: Let us draw a ship into the sea—one that has never yet made a voyage—and man her with two and fifty of our smartest young sailors.

s: Demodocus is a bard (beloved by the Muse and blind)
q: A servant presently led in the famous bard Demodocus, whom the muse had dearly loved, but to whom she had given both good and evil, for though she had endowed him with a divine gift of song, she had robbed him of his eyesight.

s: Demodocus possesses Demodocus’s lyre (his musical instrument)
q: He hung the lyre for him on a peg over his head, and showed him where he was to feel for it with his hands.

s: Muse grants divine gift of song (to Demodocus)
q: though she had endowed him with a divine gift of song, she had robbed him of his eyesight.

s: Demodocus sings Ulysses and Achilles’ quarrel (at the banquet)
q: the muse inspired Demodocus to sing the feats of heroes, and more especially a matter that was then in the mouths of all men, to wit, the quarrel between Ulysses and Achilles

s: Alcinous provides Phaeacian hospitality (for strangers who come to his house)
q: indeed, no one who ever yet came to my house has been able to complain of me for not speeding on his way soon enough.

s: Demodocus sings Mars and Venus’ affair (during the athletic games)
q: Meanwhile the bard began to sing the loves of Mars and Venus

s: sacrificial banquet includes Demodocus (as its bardic entertainment)
q: for as regards you aldermen and town councillors, you will join me in entertaining our guest in the cloisters. I can take no excuses, and we will have Demodocus to sing to us

s: sacrificial banquet includes athletic games (after the feast and minstrelsy)
q: we have had enough now, both of the feast, and of the minstrelsy that is its due accompaniment; let us proceed therefore to the athletic sports
